# Phase 5 — In-Season Program

*September 20, 2026 · Kenneth Quinones, Assistant Football Coach LB/RB, Dover High School*

This is the operational program for Phase 5 (In-Season), the fifth and final phase of the program: exercises, loads, and session structure for the week-by-week execution of the plan.

## Overview

Dates. Phase 5 begins once the 2027 regular season starts, immediately following camp, and runs through the final regular-season game. Dover's actual 2027 schedule isn't published yet, so this document uses the 2026 season as a structural reference only, not as this phase's actual dates: an 8-game schedule running from early September through a final game in the second half of October, ending before Halloween. Expect a similar shape for 2027 — roughly an 8-week season, season-opener in early September — and treat the exact dates as a placeholder to update once NJSIAA/Dover publish them. This document doesn't depend on knowing them in advance.

Camp itself is governed by NJSIAA's heat-acclimatization mandate and run by the football staff, not this S&C program. This program also covers part of camp: see the Camp Bridge section below for what resumes, and when. Phase 5's Week 1 is still the first full week that includes the season's first game — Camp Bridge covers everything between Phase 4's last session and that point.

Frequency and structure, mapped onto a typical Friday-game week. Two lift days (GD-4 and GD-2, described below), trimmed NMT before every practice day (Nordic lower and shoulder finisher on the two lift days only), no formal lifting the day before a game (GD-1, typically a walkthrough) or the day after one — see Weekly Template. For a Friday game: the day after (Saturday) is full rest or optional light recovery only; Sunday is off; Monday (GD-4, the first practice back) is Lift Day 1; Tuesday (GD-3) is practice only; Wednesday (GD-2) is Lift Day 2; Thursday (GD-1, walkthrough) has no lift. For a Thursday game, shift the whole pattern back one day. For a Saturday game, the pattern doesn't change — Friday just becomes an additional light day before kickoff.

If there's a bye week. A bye week removes a game from that week's load equation, so it isn't treated identically to a normal week. Practically: the lift days stay in place, but with one fewer high-load event that week, the sRPE/ACWR data will usually support holding load flat or nudging it up slightly rather than cutting further — the load-tracking system in Progression Scheme is what actually makes that call, not a fixed rule.

Location. Weight room for lift days; wherever the team practices for the trimmed NMT on non-lift days.

Roster and coaching staff. Same coaching staff as the rest of the program. Weight-room access has to work around the practice schedule, not the other way around — lift days are short and scheduled around whatever window practice actually leaves open that day.

Session length. Short by necessity: roughly 30–40 minutes for a lift day (~5-7 minutes trimmed NMT, 15–20 minutes for the two main lifts plus the shoulder finisher, plus about 2-3 minutes per barbell lift for its warm-up ramp; add 2-3 minutes on GD-4/GD-2 for the relocated Nordic lower - time a live session before trusting these estimates), reflecting how little time a game week actually leaves for the weight room. Non-lift practice days add only the NMT/Nordic lower/shoulder-finisher block (≈ 10–15 minutes) before the team's own practice.

NMT warm-up, Nordic hamstring lower, and shoulder-health finisher. **Revised Oct 21, 2026:** the NMT warm-up runs in the trimmed form from Phase 1 (Part 2 plus 2 build-up sprints) before every practice day, and the Nordic hamstring lower is **2 sets x 6-8 reps on GD-4 and GD-2 only, post-lift** (two sessions a week, never consecutive days; none on GD-3 or GD-1). The shoulder-health finisher continues on lift days. The stop-and-hand-off rules (concussion, injury or illness, new or persistent pain) from the Phase 1 document apply in season unchanged, and a suspected concussion follows Dover's concussion policy and the athletic trainer, not this program. Full protocols are in the Phase 1 document; not repeated here.

Heat and hydration. The season opens in early September, still warm in New Jersey. Same standard as Phase 3/4: water breaks, ice/cold-towel access, and shortening or moving a session on a flagged extreme-heat day — though by mid-season this matters less than it did in Phase 3/4's peak-summer heat.

Nutrition and sleep. Same standards as every prior phase: protein intake in the 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day range, consistent sleep in the 8–10 hour range. Both matter more, not less, with games now in the mix.

Missed-day policy — changed from every prior phase. Off-season, a missed day gets made up at reduced volume. In-season, it doesn't: total weekly load is already being tracked and managed deliberately (see Progression Scheme), so adding a makeup session on top of a game week's existing load runs against the phase's whole purpose. A missed lift day is simply missed; the sRPE/ACWR system accounts for the lighter week rather than a coach trying to claw it back.

## First-time athletes arriving after the off-season program

GD-4 and GD-2 both load against "each athlete's most recently tested e1RM" — a number that doesn't exist for an athlete who joins this late, whether that's during camp or once the season itself has started. Two separate things have to happen before this athlete lifts alongside the rest of the roster: the football staff's own contact and conditioning ramp-up (governed by NJSIAA's heat-acclimatization mandate during camp, and by ordinary coaching judgment once the season is underway) is not this program's call to make, and this document defers to it entirely for practice/contact reps. Separately and in parallel, this program's own job is narrower but non-negotiable: this athlete does not get loaded against a percentage of an e1RM that was never measured. On GD-4 and GD-2, they run the same RPE-based (Rating of Perceived Exertion, a 1-10 effort scale) technique work used everywhere earlier in this program's late-arrival chain, in place of the barbell percentage work, until a real 5RM test clears them onto the standard prescription — but **not on the same runway for every movement**. Bench/Pull-up need one clean RPE 6-7 technique session before testing; Squat/Deadlift need three, matching Phase 1's own 3-week floor for axial-loaded lifts. An athlete arriving this late will very likely clear the upper-body three well before Squat/Deadlift clears its own longer floor — that's expected, not a sign something's off, and each movement group tests and moves onto the standard prescription as soon as it individually clears, rather than waiting for both to clear together. An athlete arriving this late is, realistically, playing before that testing and technique work is fully banked; that's a roster-management and player-safety judgment call for the coaching staff to make with the football staff, not something this document can resolve from a lifting-program page. What this document can guarantee is that whenever this athlete does step under a bar, the load on it corresponds to a number that was actually tested, not an assumption inherited from a phase they were never part of — and that Squat/Deadlift specifically isn't rushed onto that number just to keep pace with the upper-body three.

## Camp Bridge (Blackout Week Through the Season Opener)

Phase 4 ends, a full no-contact blackout week follows with zero coach-led training, and camp itself then opens under NJSIAA's mandatory 14-day heat-acclimatization ramp. On the conditioning side, camp practice already includes its own conditioning, built into the practice window the same way it's always been run here. Both pieces below bridge to Phase 5's Week 1.

**Lifting.** No lifting in the first 5 days of the heat-acclimatization ramp (single practice per day, capped at 3 hours, helmets only the first two days) — the highest-risk window of the entire calendar for exertional illness, and weight-room time counts against that same capped practice-time budget, so there's no free time to add it in regardless. Once two-a-day sessions begin (Day 6 of the ramp onward), continue Phase 4 Week 2's taper-lift dose once a week, through the rest of camp:

| Exercise | Sets x Reps | % e1RM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bench Press | 2x5 | ~75% |
| **Squat** | **2x5** | **~60% — light maintenance touch, continues unchanged from Phase 3/4's Day D** |
| Pull-up (weighted, if applicable) | 2x5 | ~75% total-system-load e1RM (bodyweight + added weight; see Day D formula) |
| **Deadlift (or Trap Bar Deadlift/RDL)** | **2x5** | **~60% — same maintenance touch and reasoning as Squat above** |
| Overhead Press | 2x5 | ~75% |

Bodyweight-track Pull-up: 2x5, 2–3 reps in reserve, no added weight. Schedule it into whichever of that day's two sessions (or that week's single-practice day, on an alternating schedule) leaves the most practical window — there's no fixed day here the way Phase 3/4 has one, since camp's actual daily schedule is the football staff's to set, not this program's. **Squat and Deadlift now carry a light maintenance touch through this bridge, continuing unchanged from Phase 3 and Phase 4's Day D, rather than going fully dormant** — see Phase 5's Week 1-2 re-entry ramp (Progression Scheme) for the other half of this fix. A first-time athlete with no e1RM on file (whether arriving during camp or earlier) runs the same RPE-based technique protocol defined in "First-time athletes arriving after the off-season program" above, in place of this bridge lift.

**Conditioning.** Stays exactly where it's always been — built into the back portion of practice's existing time window, not added on top of it. Camp's end-of-practice conditioning runs on the same SIT (sprint interval training) template Phase 3's Day C already established — repeated maximal-effort 20m out-and-back shuttle sprints (40m total), not distance running, the same format this roster has already been training on for a month by the time camp opens. This isn't new content introduced at camp; it's Phase 3's own conditioning method continuing on the field it's already running on, scaled to whatever time that day's practice window actually leaves rather than Phase 3's fixed weekly 2x4/2x5 set-and-rep table — camp's practice-time budget, not a training calendar, decides daily volume here.

The staff's actual allotment is roughly 10 minutes at the end of practice. Running shuttles continuously isn't right regardless: dropping the longer between-set rest to fit more reps into a fixed window would change the stimulus (steady-state fatigue running instead of near-maximal repeated efforts) and increase heat-illness risk. Phase 3's own two-set structure (30 sec between reps, ~3 min between the two sets, +25% for linemen) is what should run, in full, regardless of position:

| Group | Sets x Reps | Rest/rep | Rest/set | Approx. total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Skill positions | 2x4 | 30 sec | 3 min | ~7 min |
| Skill positions | 2x5 | 30 sec | 3 min | ~8 min |
| Linemen (+25% recovery) | 2x4 | ~38 sec | ~3:45 | ~8.5 min |
| Linemen (+25% recovery) | 2x5 | ~38 sec | ~3:45 | ~10 min |

(Per-rep time estimated at ~7-8 sec for a clean 20m-out-and-back; coaches should time a live rep rather than trust this exactly, the same caution this program uses for every other session-length estimate.) **The 10-minute figure isn't a ceiling to engineer around - there's real slack behind it:** practice is scheduled for 2.5 hours and typically finishes around 2 once everything's complete, well inside NJSIAA's 3-hour single-practice cap (and the 5-hour combined cap once two-a-days begin). A linemen's group running its full 2x5 volume a couple minutes past the usual 10 isn't a real constraint given that margin. **Run the complete prescribed volume, full recovery intervals, for every position group, including linemen's full 2x5 - don't default-trim linemen's reps to fit a clock that has real give in it.** The rule that doesn't flex, regardless of how much time is available, is the recovery structure itself: never shorten the rest between reps or between sets to add more volume, on any day, for any group - that's a training-stimulus and heat-safety issue independent of the clock. If a specific day's practice is genuinely running up against the 3-hour ceiling for some other reason, trimming linemen to 4 reps per set (never the recovery) is the correct fallback - just not a standing default. Three refinements apply specifically to camp, all compatible with that existing structure and with the SIT template's own rules: linemen get the same recovery extension Phase 3 already prescribes for them (recovery intervals extended by roughly 25% over the prescribed rep count, not identical conditioning to skill positions) rather than a new camp-specific adjustment, carrying the existing rule forward instead of inventing a separate one; keep the heaviest-intensity version of it (the longest rep counts, shortest recovery) out of the first few days of the 14-day ramp, before pads and heat exposure have built up gradually, running a lighter rep count within the same shuttle format and letting it build back to normal established volume as the ramp progresses; and never let it run independent of the WBGT checklist already governing Phase 3/4's outdoor work — on an Orange/Red day, this is the part of practice that gets shortened or cut first, consistent with Phase 3's own Red-tier rule that SIT/sled work is the first thing cut. None of this is new volume, new time, or a new method; it's Phase 3's existing SIT conditioning segment, continuing through camp on the practice staff's own schedule rather than this program's fixed weekly table.

## Weekly Template

### GD-4 — Lift Day 1

1. NMT warm-up (trimmed, ~5-7 min), then a **warm-up ramp** on Squat and on Bench Press just before each one's work sets: 50% x5, 65% x3, 75% x2 of the athlete's e1RM, the same warm-up ramp as Phases 1-2, skipping any step at or above that week's working percentage (so Week 1's 70% uses only 50% x5 and 65% x3). Warm-up sets are not counted as work sets.
2. Squat: 3x3–5 @ ~80–85% of each athlete's most recently tested **e1RM** (Phase 2, Week 7 retest), **Heavy Maintenance pace — controlled, not a grind (not CAT; CAT stays defined at 50-70% e1RM elsewhere in this program). Weeks 1-2 of the season run a lower re-entry ramp (70% then 78% e1RM) instead — see Progression Scheme.**
3. Bench Press: 3x3–5 @ ~80–85% of each athlete's most recently tested e1RM, same Heavy Maintenance pace.
4. **Monday auto-regulation:** after a high-snap-count or physically demanding Friday game, this session lands roughly 60-65 hours post-game - still inside the 24-72 hour muscle-damage window the recovery research behind this phase's schedule cites. Default to the low end of 80-85% e1RM, or drop to 2 work sets instead of 3, based on the coaching staff's read of Friday's game and the prior week's sRPE/ACWR data (Progression Scheme). A quiet week with no unusual game toll runs the full prescription as written.
5. **Post-lift finisher:** Shoulder-health finisher (face pull or band pull-apart, 2x15–20) **then** Nordic hamstring lower (2 sets x 6-8 reps).

### GD-3 — Practice Only

Trimmed NMT warm-up (Part 2 plus 2 build-up sprints; no Nordic on this day) before practice. No barbell work.

### GD-2 — Lift Day 2

1. NMT warm-up (trimmed, ~5-7 min), then a **warm-up ramp** on the Deadlift (or RDL) just before its work sets: 50% x5, 65% x3, 75% x2 of the athlete's e1RM, the same warm-up ramp as Phases 1-2, skipping any step at or above that week's working percentage (so Week 1's 70% uses only 50% x5 and 65% x3). Warm-up sets are not counted as work sets. The Pull-up needs no ramp.
2. Deadlift (or RDL, if an athlete's technique or load management calls for it): 3x3–5 @ ~80–85% of each athlete's most recently tested **e1RM** (Phase 2, Week 7 retest), **Heavy Maintenance pace (not CAT; CAT stays defined at 50-70% e1RM elsewhere in this program). Weeks 1-2 of the season run the same re-entry ramp as GD-4's Squat (70% then 78% e1RM) — see Progression Scheme.**
3. Pull-up (weighted, if the athlete's tested baseline called for added load): 3x3–5 at ~80% of the **total-system-load** e1RM (belt/vest load = 80% x [(bodyweight + added weight at the Phase 2, Week 7 retest) ÷ 0.87] - current bodyweight, rounded to 2.5 lb; bodyweight only if that comes out at or below zero); bodyweight athletes run 3x3–5 with 2–3 reps in reserve.
4. **Post-lift finisher:** Shoulder-health finisher (2x15–20) **then** Nordic hamstring lower (2 sets x 6-8 reps).

### GD-1 — Walkthrough

Trimmed NMT warm-up (Part 2 plus 2 build-up sprints; no Nordic on this day) before the walkthrough. No barbell work, no added conditioning — this is the lightest day of the week by design.

### Game Day

No formal S&C session. NMT is the team's own pregame warm-up routine, unchanged.

### Day After Game

Full rest, or optional light mobility/NMT-only work for athletes who want it — coach-supervised but not mandatory. No lifting.

## Progression Scheme

There isn't a week-to-week progression in the usual sense for most of the season — this is a maintenance phase, and the load stays flat by design (3x3–5 @ ~80–85% of each athlete's tested e1RM, every lift day, all season) once it's up to full intensity. What actually varies week to week after that is how much total load the season is putting on each athlete, tracked through the system below — that's this phase's real "progression scheme."

**Squat and Deadlift's Week 1-2 re-entry ramp.** GD-4 (Squat) and GD-2 (Deadlift) load against each athlete's Phase 2, Week 7 e1RM — by the season opener, roughly three to four months old. The Camp Bridge's maintenance touch keeps the motor pattern alive through that stretch but doesn't refresh the number itself, and this phase deliberately doesn't add a new max-effort retest to do that (adding a maximal-exertion testing day on top of a full game schedule is exactly the stress this phase exists to avoid). Squat and Deadlift specifically (not Bench Press, which stayed current at ~75-80% throughout Phase 3/4's Day D) ramp in over the season's first two weeks: **Week 1 runs 70% e1RM, Week 2 runs 78% e1RM** (the same conservative-restart figure used elsewhere in this program after a real layoff), and **Week 3 onward runs the full 80-85% prescription** — unless that week's sRPE/ACWR data or a coach's own read says otherwise, same as any other week.

**Warm-up ramp (added Oct 4, 2026).** Squat, Bench Press and Deadlift get the same 50% x5, 65% x3, 75% x2 warm-up ramp used in Phases 1-2 before their work sets, because 80-85% sets call for it and the earlier phases already teach it; it is about 10 reps well below the working weight and is not counted as training volume. It is separate from the Week 1-2 re-entry ramp above, which changes the work-set percentage. The Phase 3 and Phase 4 maintenance lifts (about 60-80% e1RM) do not use it.

**The sRPE/ACWR protocol.**

1. Collect. Roughly 20–30 minutes after every practice, lift, and game, each athlete gives a single session-RPE rating: a 0–10 difficulty score (Borg CR-10 scale) for how hard that specific session felt. Given roster size, this is a quick verbal call-out or a simple paper/spreadsheet log per squad — not an app or a lengthy survey.
2. Calculate session load. Session load (in arbitrary units) = RPE × session duration in minutes. A lift day's duration is that day's actual 25–35 minutes; a practice or game's duration is however long that session ran.
3. Calculate weekly (acute) load. Sum every session's load for the week — practices, lifts, and the game all count.
4. Calculate chronic load. A rolling 4-week average of weekly load.
5. Calculate ACWR. Acute (this week) ÷ chronic (trailing 4-week average). 0.8–1.3 is the sweet spot; ≥1.5 is the danger zone.
6. Calculate monotony and strain (optional, if bandwidth allows). Monotony = weekly mean daily load ÷ standard deviation of daily loads within that week; strain = weekly load × monotony. A week that's both high-load and low-variation (every day feels about the same, nothing lighter to recover into) is a higher-risk week even if the raw ACWR looks fine.

**A caveat on the ACWR number.** Because the acute week's load is also part of the chronic average, the ratio's own math can produce coupling artifacts that look like a meaningful signal even when they aren't — ACWR's predictive power for an individual athlete's injury risk is weaker than the >1.5 danger-zone framing implies. This program still uses ACWR because it's simple enough for a two-person coaching staff to calculate by hand every week and act on immediately. But treat it as a rough, easy-to-compute prompt for a coach's attention, not a validated clinical predictor, and lean on the monotony/strain numbers in step 6 as a useful second check, since they aren't built on the same self-referential ratio — a high-strain week is worth flagging even when ACWR alone looks fine, and a borderline ACWR reading is worth weighing against a coach's own read of the athlete before changing anything.

What the numbers actually change. The coaching staff reviews the prior week's numbers before setting that week's lift loads. An ACWR pushing toward or past 1.5, or a high-strain week, is the signal to hold or reduce GD-4/GD-2 lift loads that week — drop to 2x3–5 or trim intensity slightly — never to add anything on top. A quiet week (ACWR well inside the sweet spot) is not, by itself, a reason to push harder; this remains a maintenance phase regardless of what the data shows on a good week.

Auto-regulation. Same standard as every prior phase: if an athlete's technique breaks down under the prescribed load, drop it 5–10% rather than grinding the rep. In-season, err toward less on any day a coach's own read of an athlete — flat, banged up, playing heavy snap counts — disagrees with what the load numbers say; the numbers support a coach's judgment here, they don't replace it.

## Equipment Substitutions

| Called for | If unavailable, substitute |
| --- | --- |
| Squat rack / platform | Same weight-room equipment already established in Phase 1–2; nothing new needed for this phase |
| Deadlift platform | A cleared, flat section of weight-room floor with bumper plates works if a dedicated platform isn't available |
| Pull-up bar | Same as Phase 1–3 |
| Timer (for session-duration tracking) | Any phone or watch timer — needed for the sRPE load calculation above, not for testing |
